title: Next Tick of a Cell Colony
statement:
A colony lives on an m × n grid. Each cell is alive (1) or dead (0). A cell's neighbours are the up to 8 cells around it, including diagonals. Cells outside the grid count as dead.

All cells update at the same moment, based only on the old grid:

  • A live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive. With fewer or more, it dies.
  • A dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours comes alive. Otherwise it stays dead.

Update grid in place to the next state. Return nothing; the grid itself is checked.

examples.why: A vertical bar of three turns horizontal. The middle cell keeps 2 neighbours; the side cells of the middle row each see 3.
The empty corner sees 3 live neighbours and is born. Writing the update straight into the grid cell by cell would change the counts for cells read later.
The ends have only one neighbour each and die; the inner two have two and survive.

hints: Why can't you just loop over the cells and overwrite each one as you go?
With a copy of the old grid the rules are direct. To avoid the copy, each cell needs to remember both its old and its new state at the same time.
Store the next state in a second bit: grid[i][j] |= 2 when the cell will be alive. Count neighbours with grid[x][y] & 1, then shift every cell right by one at the end.

explain.intuition:
Every cell must be judged against the old generation. If you overwrite a cell and then count it as a neighbour of the next cell, you are mixing two generations. The simple fix is to count against a copy of the grid.

To drop the copy, note each cell only holds 0 or 1, so the integer has spare bits. Keep the old state in bit 0 and write the new state into bit 1. Neighbour counts read cell & 1, which is unaffected by bit 1. When every cell has its next state recorded, one more pass shifts each cell right to make bit 1 the current state. This is the same idea as double-buffering a canvas: compute the next frame without disturbing the one on screen, then swap.
steps: For each cell, count live neighbours with grid[x][y] & 1 over the up to 8 surrounding cells.
If the cell is alive and has 2 or 3 live neighbours, or is dead and has exactly 3, set grid[i][j] |= 2.
After the full pass, replace every cell with grid[i][j] >> 1.
pitfalls: Updating cells in place without a copy or extra bit, as the second example shows.
Counting the cell itself as one of its own neighbours.
Reading neighbours with grid[x][y] === 1 after some cells already hold 2 or 3. Use & 1.

solutions.title: Count against a copy
solutions.idea: Copy the grid, then compute each new cell from the copy so every count uses the old generation.

solutions.title: Second bit holds the next state
solutions.idea: Bit 0 keeps the current state for neighbour counts, bit 1 records the next state. A final pass shifts right.

followups: The board is infinite and only a few thousand cells are alive. How do you store it and compute the next tick?
The grid is too large for memory and arrives row by row. How many rows do you need to hold at once?
